Ok, I'll just paste the ideation we had: "Of these two challenges, which one do you think fits us as a group (same as in Zürich better)? Just some first ideas, context, background, and recommendation.

Read 3 memories
Good context to work with here, given how the Munich stop actually went for you and the team.
Quick read on the two options: the BMW routing challenge is a personalization/data-product problem — GPS tracks, motorcycle sensor data (speed, G-force, lean angle), rider profiles, and an open invitation to bolt on weather, traffic, or scenic-viewpoint data. The scoring is subjective ("you define fun, we evaluate"), which means it rewards a working, well-demoed prototype more than methodological rigor. The Temporal AI Challenge is a different animal: source/validate a dataset (possibly via an agentic pipeline), build or use a TimeNet connector, then actually train or fine-tune a time-series language model and benchmark it against a baseline on held-out data with proper leakage controls across time/subjects/devices. That's a research deliverable, not a hack.
Given what worked for your team in Munich, I'd lean toward the BMW challenge. Your QuantCo run was won on exactly the BMW challenge's terms: ship something rough but working early, lean on an LLM-first architecture with a knowledge base to cover sparse data, iterate fast, and you clearly have the pitching chops (finalist stage, co-presenting) to make a subjectively-judged "most exciting solution" metric work in your favor. The BMW brief practically invites that playbook again: creative enrichment layers (weather, scenic routing) are cheap wins for a flashy demo, and there's a nice map visualization angle built in.
The Temporal Challenge is the one that's actually closer to your own expertise, worth naming honestly: dataset sourcing pipelines, avoiding leakage across time/subjects, comparing against baselines on held-out data is more or less what you do on HANCAS day to day (you literally caught and fixed a leakage-adjacent bug in your thesis pipeline a few weeks back). If you specifically wanted a hackathon that doubles as thesis-adjacent practice or you have someone on the team who can move fast on fine-tuning with compute already lined up, it's a legitimate pull. But in a 24h window I'd flag it as the higher-variance choice: training and properly evaluating a TSLM in a day, without pre-arranged compute, is ambitious, and the risk is you end up with an unfinished pipeline and nothing compelling to demo, whereas your team's Munich edge came specifically from always having a working, positive submission on the board.
So: BMW route challenge as the safer, form-matching pick given how your team actually won last time; Temporal AI Challenge only if someone's itching for the research angle and you're confident about compute/time budget for the training step.
for the temporal one: It is also about getting a dataset etc. Do you have ideas? Maybe also medical angle? HANCOCK would not qualify, would it?

Read 4 pages, searched the web, loaded tools
Confirmed: HANCOCK wouldn't be a natural fit here, and not because of access (it's fully open, CC BY 4.0, downloadable via TCIA). The blood work and clinical labs are single pre-operative snapshots, not repeated measurements, so there's no per-patient longitudinal signal to feed a time-series model. Survival/recurrence is a time-to-event outcome (one number per patient, right-censored), not a time series either. It's a strong multimodal dataset (WSIs, TMAs, tabular clinical/lab data, surgery reports) but it's static-plus-imaging, not the "signal stream + text reasoning over it" shape the challenge's own "Ideal Data Profile" slide calls for.
Worth noting: that slide's "as in OpenTSLM paper" line points to a real, very recent paper (Oct 2025, Stanford/ETH group, ICML 2026), and it names exactly the kind of datasets that would qualify. It introduces three text+time-series benchmarks: HAR-CoT (wearable activity sensors), Sleep-CoT (PSG/sleep staging), and ECG-QA-CoT (ECG + clinical QA with chain-of-thought reasoning). That's basically the organizers showing you their reference implementation.
For a medical angle with realistic 24h feasibility, I'd rank it like this:
ECG-QA on PTB-XL is probably your best shot. PTB-XL is a large, genuinely open (no credentialing wall) 12-lead ECG dataset with diagnostic labels, and ECG-QA is an existing open repo of QA pairs built on top of it, with code already on GitHub. Using one of the organizers' own reference datasets means you're not burning hackathon hours on data wrangling, you can spend the time on the actual connector + fine-tuning + eval loop, and you could still differentiate by picking a specific target user (e.g. a rural GP without cardiology backup, or post-op monitoring) and a held-out split that stresses generalization across devices or patients, which directly hits their "avoiding leakage" evaluation criterion.
Sleep-CoT-style data is a second option if someone on the team wants to frame around sleep/recovery, but the go-to source (SHHS via the National Sleep Research Resource) usually needs a data use agreement, which is friction you don't want mid-hackathon.
Wearable HAR/vitals data (PAMAP2, WISDM, or WESAD for stress/physiological signals) is a third lane if you want to frame it around rehab, elderly fall-risk, or stress monitoring rather than strictly clinical diagnostics. These are unrestricted downloads and pair naturally with a "target user" story (physiotherapist, caregiver), though you'd have to write the text-pairing/QA layer yourself since it doesn't exist off the shelf like ECG-QA does.
Given the 24h budget, I'd steer toward ECG-QA/PTB-XL specifically because it removes the biggest risk (data sourcing and QA-pairing eating half your time) and lets you spend the hackathon on the part that actually differentiates you: the TimeNet connector, the fine-tune, and a clean baseline comparison.

HANCOCK - The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA)
OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data (arXiv)
PTB-XL, a large publicly available electrocardiography dataset (PhysioNet)
ECG-QA GitHub repository

Read memory
Reading it as: more candidate datasets, checked against the full ts_gym list, that aren't SHL/SisFall/DB delay either — a bigger bench of options rather than just those three. Here's what's genuinely clear on both counts:

Rail/transit-adjacent infrastructure, to sit next to DB delay data — OpenSky Network (ADS-B flight trajectories) is a genuinely different mobility domain, more distant than AIS ships. DWD (Deutscher Wetterdienst) station data is the German analogue of the MeteoSwiss idea, absent from the list the same way.
Industrial/machines — IMS Bearing (Cincinnati run-to-failure) is a clean alternative to CWRU/C-MAPSS, not on the loader. SECOM (UCI semiconductor manufacturing, anomaly/yield) is also absent.
Clinical — MIMIC-IV waveform and PhysioNet Challenge 2020 12-lead ECG are both absent from the list, but they're canonical enough in the clinical-ML world that other teams could land on them without needing a loader either, so weaker differentiation than the industrial/rail options above.
Astronomy — Kepler/TESS transit light curves are a different task (planet detection vs. variable-star classification) from the ASAS-SN/ZTF entries already on the list, and absent themselves.
Everything above I checked line-by-line against the 79-line ts_gym corpus list already in hand — none of these appear on it, and none overlap with SHL, SisFall, or DB delay data. Want these folded into the "Off the Loader" page as a reserve-options section, or kept as a working list for now?
And seeing all of that, how is the train one?

Loaded tools, searched the web, read a page
Confirmed the differentiation held (no rail dataset anywhere on the ts_gym list, closest is ship AIS), and checked how it'd actually get built, which changes the risk picture.
There's a ready-made Hugging Face dataset for exactly this: piebro/deutsche-bahn-data, scraped historical DB operations data — 16-column monthly parquet with station, train type/number, line, delay in minutes, planned vs. actual times, and cancellation flags per stop, at 100M–1B records, CC BY 4.0, loadable straight through datasets.load_dataset (or Dask/Polars). That's the same shape as capture24 on the provided list, which is also pulled from a local HF mirror rather than scraped live — so a DB loader would be no harder to write than the ones everyone else gets handed, it just isn't handed to them. A few Kaggle mirrors (nokkyu, santiagoravotti, ravisingh0399) exist as backup or cross-check. The official live Timetables API (DBOpenData/openbahn) is real too, but needs a key from DB's developer portal — not worth the registration lag inside a 24-hour build, so the static parquet dump is the pragmatic path, not the live feed.

Trains and Delays Deutsche Bahn (Kaggle)
DBOpenData (GitHub)

=== README ===
# temporal_ai_error404.ai=== AGENTS ===
# AGENTS.md — hack-os shared agent instructions

Single source of truth for every coding harness. `CLAUDE.md` points here.
Read this whole file once per session. These rules govern product work;
explicitly requested maintenance of hack-os itself is not constrained by
an example product's demo script or contract.

## 1. Boot sequence and freshness

If `.hackos-user` is absent, run `./bootstrap.sh --auto` once. Bootstrap is
local-only: no downloads, product dependency installs, git config changes,
or credentials. Missing tools warn; markdown remains usable. Identity not
matched to the roster is unconfirmed: ask the human, never assume ownership.
MCP authentication and personal API keys are optional, per-person setup.

Read `team-setup/state/event.json` first. `mode: example`, or a legacy
`_comment` containing `WORKED EXAMPLE` without an explicit mode, means NO
active event. Say "No active event; fictional examples are inactive."
A blank `event_name` also means no active event, regardless of mode; report
"No event configured" and do not load placeholder state as requirements.
Do not load fictional challenges, contracts, owners, tasks, or decisions as
requirements. Never silently initialize or reset an event.
The distributed template keeps event records and shared session logs empty.
Keep the reusable roster in `team.json`; assign product roles fresh per event.

For an active event, read in order:
1. `team-setup/state/pipeline.json`
2. `team-setup/state/decisions.md` — identify current, non-superseded decisions.
3. `team-setup/state/owners.md`
4. `team-setup/board/tasks.json` — identify the relevant task and accountable owner.
5. `team-setup/state/01-challenge-pick/challenge.md`
6. `team-setup/state/02-demo-script/demo-script.md`
7. `team-setup/state/02-demo-script/not-building.md`
8. `team-setup/state/03-contract-freeze/contract.md`
Load `ideas.md`, `research.json`, and supporting notes when relevant.
Any document marked `WORKED EXAMPLE` is illustrative, never active scope.

State the active stage, your confirmed ownership, current task/decisions,
and whether the real contract is frozen. Missing information is unknown,
not permission to invent assignments or implement fictional requirements.

Before a new task or substantial edit, reread decisions, ownership, the
relevant task and contract. After a teammate reports a change, refresh even
in a running session. A dashboard refresh does not refresh an agent's mind.

Git is explicit synchronization, not live collaboration. `event.json`
names the coordination branch and maintainer. The maintainer integrates
accepted state changes there; teammates fetch and safely integrate before
new work and at checkpoints. Never auto-pull into a dirty worktree, discard
changes, auto-stash, or resolve another person's conflicts. Show local HEAD,
uncommitted coordination edits, and remote freshness as unknown until checked.
Offline work uses a local snapshot, never a claimed live team state.

## 2. Hackathon mode

- Write smoke tests for the demo happy path and coordination data safety.
- Do not add unit tests for unrelated product code or refactor working code.
- No speculative abstractions, new dashboards, providers, or services.
- Core storage/API stays Python 3 stdlib plus Git. The dashboard UI uses
  Vite, React, Tailwind and shadcn/ui in `team-setup/board/web/`; its Node
  dependencies are separate from whichever product stack the team chooses.
- Optional MCPs, plugins, prompt logging, and agent teams are not prerequisites.
- Vendored skills are optional; these repository rules override their workflow
  defaults. A skill does not authorize unrequested installs, data uploads,
  extra agents, destructive commands, or changes to system security controls.

## 3. Ownership rule

Before editing, check `team-setup/state/owners.md` and the owning task in
`team-setup/board/tasks.json`. Do not edit another person's assigned files.
A sub-owner helps within an explicitly delegated boundary; they do not
redirect scope. Name owners for shared wiring, manifests and lockfiles too.
Ownership is per event, not inferred from background. Use one branch/worktree
per independent writer; worktrees alone do not sync different machines.
Reassignments and delegation must be explicit and synced before work starts.
Avoid direct file editing while a dashboard write touches the same records.

## 4. Contract rule

The real `team-setup/state/03-contract-freeze/contract.md` freezes when that
gate completes. Code against it and mock missing dependencies. A required
contract change needs explicit human approval and a recorded decision.
`app/shared/` is generated from the agreed contract, never independently
patched. No sample schema, endpoint, or product stack is a requirement.

## 5. Scope rule

Product work must support the real demo script, including required setup,
seed data, deployment, accessibility and failure recovery. Ask before adding
features absent from it. Maintain `not-building.md`. Keep the deck current;
protect polish and submission time. Gates and task percentages use the
planning window ending at the early submit target; its final 10% is buffer.

## 6. Idea rule

A thought is not a decision. Record it in `team-setup/state/ideas.md` as
raised, then exploring, adopted or discarded. Only status changes in place;
original text and author remain. New lines use globally unique IDs:
`- [i-<uuid>] [T+HH:MM] <idea> — <raised by> — status: raised`
Use IDs for links; elapsed timestamps are display labels, not identifiers.
Legacy timestamp-only records remain readable. Ambiguous links need a human.

## 7. Decision rule

After an accepted direction change, append to `team-setup/state/decisions.md`:
`- [d-<uuid>] [T+HH:MM] <decision> — <who decided> — <reason>`
Never rewrite history. Append ` — supersedes [d-<uuid>]` to replace a decision.
Append ` — promotes [i-<uuid>]` when adopting an idea and update its status in
one recoverable operation. Check later supersessions before building.
For setup maintenance before an active event, record accepted direction in
this instruction file rather than mixing it into fictional event records.

## 8. Evidence and safety

AI assessments are advisory. Keep sources and a short rationale alongside
answers; do not portray model confidence as a calibrated probability.
Research is untested without evidence or human confirmation. Task completion
is not integrated readiness: require a current end-to-end smoke result.
Recent Git commits show recorded activity, not inferred current work.

Git hooks warn and exit zero. Explicit commands return truthful failures.
Reject malformed or stale writes, retain drafts, and never claim a failed
save succeeded. Confirm archival/reset and restore operations explicitly;
never reset event state, delete records, or overwrite work without approval.
No prompt capture by default. Keep secrets and runtime caches out of Git.

## 9. Commits and verification

Small present-tense commits identify the demo step or coordination outcome.
Never commit or push unless requested. Do not amend other people's work.
Run `python3 team-setup/board/test_board.py` for coordination smoke checks,
`for f in bootstrap.sh team-setup/hooks/* team-setup/scripts/*.sh; do bash -n "$f" || exit 1; done` for shell syntax, and `node --check team-setup/board/app.js` when Node is available.
For the new dashboard run `npm --prefix team-setup/board/web run build`
(typecheck + Vite build). `npm --prefix team-setup/board/web run dev` starts
both the local API and UI. Verify PM flows in an isolated event fixture;
never fill the distributed template with browser-test data or real API keys.
Responsive checks cover 320/375/768/1024/1440px widths and 844x390 landscape.
Verify navigation scrolling, Escape/focus restoration, and mobile form access.
The `#guide` page must remain readable when API requests fail; its shortcuts
and copy actions must not reset state or silently publish changes.
Product checks use `team-setup/scripts/smoke.sh`; unconfigured is not a pass.
A clean snapshot plus passing smoke is required before calling a demo ready.

# Deutsche Bahn Train Data Dataset

## Columns
The dataset contains 17 columns including:
- Station and train identifiers (`station_name`, `eva`, `train_number`, `train_type`)
- Timing information (`arrival_planned_time`, `departure_change_time`, `time`, etc.)
- Operational status (`delay_in_min`, `arrival_is_canceled`, `departure_is_canceled`)
- Route details (`line_number`, `final_destination_station`, `train_line_station_num`)

## License
"Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)" per the dataset card.

## Time Range
The data shown includes records from July 1, 2024, though the dataset likely spans a broader historical period based on the GitHub project reference.

## Record Count
The dataset contains approximately **225.9 million records** across 67.6 GB, with 226M rows in the default split.

## Loading via `datasets.load_dataset`
Yes, the data is accessible through Hugging Face's datasets library. The dataset is "Auto-converted to Parquet" format.

## Format & Partitioning
- **Format**: Parquet files
- **Processing**: Monthly files organized as `data-YYYY-MM.parquet`
- **Raw data**: Partitioned by `year/month/day/` with hourly data files

content.text:
Verified the Deutsche Bahn source before judging it. It is real and bigger than the paste says.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rows | 226M |
| Size | 67.6 GB |
| License | CC BY 4.0 |
| Layout | monthly parquet, 17 columns |

Use Polars or DuckDB over the monthly files, not pandas, and subsample in the first hour.

The strongest objection is one the paste does not raise: the unit of analysis. Delay across a single train run is roughly ten to thirty irregularly spaced points. A patch encoder is built for dense signals, so a plain baseline that lists those numbers as text in the prompt will probably match or beat your connector. That would leave the architecture with no reason to exist, in front of judges whose whole challenge is temporal modeling. The fix is to make the series station or line delay over time, hourly across months. That version is dense, seasonal, multivariate, and genuinely needs a temporal model.

Second, the advice reversed its own risk logic between messages. It picked ECG-QA specifically to avoid spending hackathon hours on data preparation, then accepted a dataset with no question-answer layer and called that scoped. Authoring both the questions and the answers also weakens the headline claim, because beating a baseline on ground truth you wrote yourself is much less convincing than beating one on labels someone else published.

What the train pick genuinely wins on:

- **Leakage.** Splitting by time and by line or station is easy to explain and directly answers the criterion the rubric names. Without the line split, the model just memorizes which routes run late.
- **Differentiation.** Absence from the provided loader list is weaker evidence than the paste treats it as, but rail really is an unoccupied domain.
- **Pitch.** German rail punctuality in front of a Zürich audience is a memorable hook, and Swiss open data gives you a comparison axis.

The question nobody answered across all three messages is compute for the fine-tune. That is the actual go or no-go for this challenge, and it outranks dataset choice.

My call: the train dataset works if you reframe the series as station or line over time and have compute settled. If compute is uncertain, the earlier ECG-QA recommendation on PTB-XL remains the lower-variance pick. Running both as a safety plus differentiator pair does not fit in a day, so commit to one.

Nothing here is recorded in the repo yet. Say the word and I will log these as raised ideas in the ideas file, which is what the repo rules expect before any of it becomes a decision.

message.content: What would be a MVP we could ship of the train data?

content.text:
An MVP that hits every rubric line: pick a station, see its hourly delay curve, ask one of three questions, and watch the fine-tuned model answer beside two baselines, with a four-cell generalization grid behind it.

## What ships

**The series.** Filter to roughly eighty busy stations over six months, aggregate to hourly, and keep three channels: mean delay in minutes, cancellation rate, and trains per hour. Context window of one week is 168 points, which patches cleanly. That slice is a few hundred thousand rows, so it fits in memory after one DuckDB pass over the monthly parquet.

**The questions, generated not written.** This is the part that answers the objection from last turn. Write question templates, then compute each answer with a deterministic function over the future window. The label is objective even though the question is yours. Three types are enough:

- Mean delay over the next six hours, scored by mean absolute error.
- Whether the next day is worse than the trailing four-week average, scored by accuracy.
- Which hour of the next day peaks, scored as a 24-way classification.

**The model.** Freeze a small base language model and train only the projection from patch embeddings into its token space, which is the connector. Add LoRA only if time remains. Do not pretrain anything.

**The baselines.** Seasonal naive using the same hour last week, majority class for the binary question, and most importantly the same base model given the identical numbers serialized as text with no connector. That third one is the comparison that proves the connector earns its place, and it is the one judges will ask about.

## How you prove it

Report all four cells, not just the best one. The gap between them is your leakage evidence.

| | Training months | Future months |
|---|---|---|
| **Stations seen in training** | memorization ceiling | temporal generalization |
| **Stations held out entirely** | entity generalization | the honest number |

Leave a one-week embargo between train and test so no context window straddles the boundary.

## Timeline

| Hours | Work |
|---|---|
| 0 to 3 | DuckDB slice, hourly aggregation, splits frozen and written to disk |
| 3 to 6 | QA generator plus all three baselines running end to end |
| 6 to 8 | Submission-ready with baselines only, nothing else touched |
| 8 to 16 | Connector training and the eval grid |
| 16 to 20 | Demo interface and the deck |
| 20 to 22 | Buffer and dry run |

The hour-eight checkpoint matters most. A baseline-only submission on the board is your floor, and it is the same move that carried your team in Munich.

Cut explicitly, in the not-building file: live timetable API, weather joins, network graph effects, per-train-run sequences, and any fourth question type.

The plan assumes one GPU is available from hour eight. If that is not settled, the connector step is where this fails, and the pitch becomes baselines plus a good eval design.

Say the word and I will record this in the ideas file and draft the not-building list.

lastPrompt: Let's do this. Also: Is there a way to only get a subset of the dataset to download first? Or do we have to download everything?

content.text:
You do not have to download anything. Three options, cheapest first.

**Query it in place.** DuckDB with httpfs reads the parquet over HTTP range requests and only pulls the columns and row groups it needs. I tested this against the July 2024 file: a filtered station aggregate returned in two seconds, no local copy.

```sql
INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
SELECT station_name, date_trunc('hour', time) AS h,
       avg(delay_in_min) AS mean_delay, count(*) AS trains
FROM read_parquet('https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/monthly_processed_data/data-2026-03.parquet')
WHERE station_name IN ('Hamburg Hbf','Köln Hbf','München Hbf')
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

**Fetch single months.** Each month is one file, so `hf download piebro/deutsche-bahn-data --include "monthly_processed_data/data-2026-0*.parquet" --repo-type dataset` gets exactly what you name. The datasets library takes the same via `data_files`.

**Skip the raw partition.** That directory is where nearly all the bulk lives and it holds nothing the slice needs.

| Piece | Size |
|---|---|
| Whole repo including raw | 67.6 GB |
| All 26 processed monthly files | 7.7 GB |
| One month in 2024 | 0.11 GB |
| One month in 2026 | 0.60 GB |
| Six recent months for the MVP | 3.5 GB |

Coverage runs from July 2024 to August 2026. One thing worth acting on: the monthly files grow more than fivefold across that span, which means station coverage expanded over time rather than traffic increasing. If you train on 2024 and test on 2026 you are measuring a coverage change and a temporal shift at once. Take six consecutive recent months so density stays stable.

The schema also confirms the plan works. There is a per-stop timestamp for hourly aggregation, integer delay in minutes, separate arrival and departure cancellation flags, and a ride identifier with stop sequence numbers if you ever want the per-run view back.

## Recorded

Ten entries are now in the ideas file, covering the dataset, the reframe to hourly station series, the slice, the deterministic question generation, the three question types, the text baseline, the leakage grid, the hour-eight floor, the fallback, and the compute blocker. The dataset and the reframe are marked exploring, the rest raised. The cut list is drafted in the not-building file as eight rows with reasons.

Three things I deliberately did not do. No entry in the decisions file, because one person saying yes is not a recorded team decision and the repo treats those separately. No event initialization, since the event name is still blank. Nothing committed.

Also note the local identity file reads unconfirmed, so I attributed the ideas to you by name without assigning you ownership of anything.

# Connector anatomy

Deep reference for the `add-dataset-connector` skill. Everything here is verified against the code on
this branch. Anchor files:

- Contract: `packages/timenet/src/timenet/connectors/base.py`
- Bases: `packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/bases/{huggingface,physionet}.py`
- Discovery: `packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/discovery.py`
- Build CLI: `packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/builder/cli.py`
- Worked examples: the `chengsenwang/tsqa`, `physionet/ecg_qa_cot`, and `timenet/hello_world` connectors

## The `BaseConnector` contract

`BaseConnector(ABC, Generic[TRaw])` in `timenet.connectors`. `TRaw` is whatever `download` hands to
`convert` (a dict per Hub row, a dataclass ref per PhysioNet record, etc.).

- `download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]` (abstract): fetch/discover raw source files, return
  lightweight refs. I/O only, no parsing, idempotent for a given `cache_dir`.
- `convert(self, raw_refs: list[TRaw]) -> TimeFDataset` (abstract): parse refs into a `TimeFDataset`.
  CPU only, no network.
- `metadata(self) -> DatasetMetadata` (**concrete**, do not override): loads and validates the card via
  `DatasetMetadata.from_yaml`. By convention the card is `dataset.yaml` beside the connector module;
  set the `CARD` class var to point elsewhere. (Some docs call `metadata` abstract; it isn't.)
- `store(...)` (concrete): derives the schema if missing and streams the dataset through `TimeFWriter`.
  Most connectors never override it.

Connectors take **no constructor arguments** (configuration comes from the environment). End with a
module-level `CONNECTOR = <YourClass>`.

## Discovery and the folder layout

A connector is a package folder, not a flat file:

```
packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/datasets/<org>/<name>/
  __init__.py      # re-exports CONNECTOR (and the class) from connector.py
  connector.py     # the BaseConnector subclass; ends with CONNECTOR = <YourClass>
  dataset.yaml     # the dataset card, read by metadata()
  requirements.txt # the libraries this connector needs, installed into the
                   # environment its build runs in (optional)
```

`discovery.resolve(dataset_id)` imports only the one module and reads its `CONNECTOR`.
`discovery._module_name` maps the id to the module path: org lowercased, leaf hyphens to underscores, so
`chengsenwang/tsqa -> ...datasets.chengsenwang.tsqa` and `physionet/ecg-qa-cot -> ...datasets.physionet.ecg_qa_cot`.
The org folder needs its own `__init__.py` (a namespace package that exposes no `CONNECTOR`).

## The dataset card (`dataset.yaml`)

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://docs.timenet.ai/schemas/dataset-card-v1.schema.json
yaml_schema_version: 1
dataset_id: chengsenwang/tsqa
dataset_version: 1.0.0
name: TSQA
description: "Time-series question answering: a series plus a question/answer per record."
license: Apache-2.0
domains:
  - general
tags:
  - qa
  - time-series
  - huggingface
```

`dataset_id` must equal the id the connector is built under. `license` must be a valid `License`;
`domains` valid `Domain` values. The card is validated on load (needs the `build` extra, which
`timenet[build]` pulls in); errors raise `TimeNetInvalidCardError`.

## Base connectors to reuse

### `BaseHuggingFaceConnector` (`bases/huggingface.py`)
`BaseHuggingFaceConnector(BaseConnector[dict[str, Any]])`. Set `HF_REPO` to the external Hub repo id
and implement `convert`. `download` is inherited: it reads the Hub's auto-converted parquet on
`refs/convert/parquet` and returns one dict per row, so any source format is handled uniformly.
The connector imports `huggingface_hub` lazily and declares it in its `requirements.txt`. The lazy
import keeps `--no-isolation` usable while you write the connector. `HF_TOKEN` is read from the
environment, so gated datasets work. Fully private repos have no auto-parquet ref and aren't supported.

### `BasePhysioNetConnector` (`bases/physionet.py`)
`BasePhysioNetConnector(BaseConnector[TRaw])`. Implement `download` and `convert`. Its two helpers read
records through `wfdb`, which the base imports lazily so that `--no-isolation` stays usable while you
write the connector:
- `_read_header(record_base)`: WFDB header (`fs`, `sig_len`, `sig_name`), no signal decode.
- `_lead_loader(record_base, lead_idx) -> Callable[[], pa.Array]`: lazy float32 loader for one lead's
  physical signal.

The base does not fetch the archive. Call `ensure_archive` / `download_files` from
`timenet_connectors.download`. The connector's `requirements.txt` then declares `wfdb` plus whatever
its download path needs. `physionet/ecg_qa_cot` pulls PTB-XL from `s3://physionet-open/`, which goes
through boto3, so it names `boto3` too.

## Building the dataset in `convert`

Populate a `TimeFDataset` (`from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries`):

- `TimeSeries.from_values(values, *, spec, signal, time_axis, source_id=None, time_series_id=None)`
  is the shortcut when you already hold the values in memory: it wraps them in a **float32** loader and
  takes `n_values` from the array's own length. When the source has one arbitrary time offset per point,
  use `TimeSeries.from_irregular(values, *, time_offsets_us, spec, signal, ...)` instead, which derives
  the axis from the stream. Use the raw `TimeSeries(..., loader=<Callable[[], pa.Array]>, ...)`
  constructor only for genuinely lazy sources (files, remote shards). `time_series_id` is the dedupe key:
  reuse the same id (and the same `TimeSeries`) to share one series across records.
- `spec` is a `TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type=..., name=..., unit_value=ureg.<unit>, data_source=...)`.
  Units come from the shared pint registry `ureg` (`from timenet.types import ureg`). Optional
  `data_source=DataSource(data_source_type=..., name=..., provider=...)`.
- `record = dataset.add_record(time_series=<tuple of TimeSeries>, record_id=...)`. A windowed record
  says so through its axis: `RegularAxis.at_index(...)` moves the origin into the recording.
- `record.add_annotation(Annotation(key=..., value=..., id=...))` attaches one and returns it;
  `record.add_annotations([...])` takes an iterable and returns a tuple. One class: its shape comes from
  its `span`. No span means whole-record; `span=TimePoint.seconds(...)` a time offset;
  `span=TimeInterval.seconds(...)` a region.
- `dataset.add_task(record, <Task>(...))` registers one and returns it; `dataset.add_tasks(record, [...])`
  takes an iterable and registers the batch all-or-nothing. Set `scope` and `from_tasks` on the task
  itself, not the call; a batch may derive from its own members in any order.
- Name any annotation or task you reference later and read its `id` off it. Never repeat an id literal in
  `input_annotation_ids`, `target_annotation_ids`, or `from_tasks`.

## Task types (`timenet.types.tasks`)

The task **class** is the type tag (used by `search(task=...)`); the instance carries the payload.

Every task shares one frame on the `Task` base — `record_ids`, `prompt`, `scope` (a `Span` narrowing the
input), `input_annotation_ids`, `target` / `target_annotation_ids`, `rationale`, `from_tasks` — so the
type only says what *kind* of answer it is.

| Task | Answer | Extra payload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ClassificationTask` | `target: str` (a label) | optional `target_schema` |
| `AnswerTask` | `target: str` (free text; a caption when there is no `prompt`) | — |
| `ScalarPredictionTask` | `target: float` | optional `unit`, `target_name` |
| `TemporalLocalizationTask` | `target: tuple[Span, ...]` | `mode` (`SPARSE` / `EXHAUSTIVE`) |
| `ForecastingTask` | the produced series | `context_record_ids`, `target_record_id` |
| `TSEditingTask` | the produced series | `source_record_id`, `target_record_id` |
| `TSGenerationTask` | the produced series | `target_record_id` |
| `TSCorrespondenceTask` | `target: tuple[str, ...]` (record ids) | `candidate_record_ids` |

The three series-output tasks set `answer_is_record` and locate their answer by record id instead of
filling `target`. Every other task needs exactly one of `target` or `target_annotation_ids` (the latter
points at stored annotations instead of copying them into the task row); `add_task` enforces that, plus
the bounds of every `Span` the task carries.

######## hello_world connector.py ########
"""A synthetic, offline connector that tests every TimeF feature.

``HelloWorldConnector`` needs no network. It creates a fully deterministic dataset. The writer and
reader test suites use this dataset as a fixture for round-trip tests. The connector covers two
modalities, a shared data source, a series shared across records, and a windowed record. It also
covers a longer series. The writer tests split this longer series into chunks under a small chunk
cap. The connector covers all three annotation shapes, including one shared across records, and a
task chain.
"""

from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

from jaxtyping import Float, Float64
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

from timenet.connectors import BaseConnector
from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries
from timenet.dataset.axis import RegularAxis
from timenet.types import (
    Annotation,
    AnswerTask,
    ClassificationTask,
    DataSource,
    LocalizationMode,
    ScalarPredictionTask,
    TemporalLocalizationTask,
    TimeInterval,
    TimePoint,
    TimeSeriesSpec,
    ureg,
)


_SAMPLING_RATE_HZ = 16.0
_AXIS = RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(16)
_SOURCE = DataSource(data_source_type="synthetic", name="Synthetic Generator", provider="TimeNet")
_SINE = TimeSeriesSpec(
    spec_type="sine",
    name="Sine",
    unit_value=ureg.dimensionless,
    data_source=_SOURCE,
)
_COSINE = TimeSeriesSpec(
    spec_type="cosine",
    name="Cosine",
    unit_value=ureg.dimensionless,
    data_source=_SOURCE,
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class HelloWorldRecording:
    """A lightweight, deterministic description of one synthetic recording."""

    index: int
    n_values: int


def _wave_values(
    fn: Callable[[Float64[np.ndarray, " time"]], Float[np.ndarray, " time"]], n: int, phase: float
) -> Float[np.ndarray, " time"]:
    """Compute a closed-form wave as an array.

    The function does not use a random number generator or perform I/O.

    Args:
        fn: The wave function to apply to the angular time base, for example ``np.sin``.
        n: The number of samples.
        phase: The phase offset in radians.

    Returns:
        The wave values as a float32 ``np.ndarray``.
    """
    t = np.arange(n, dtype=np.float64) / _SAMPLING_RATE_HZ
    return fn(2.0 * np.pi * t + phase).astype(np.float32)


def _wave(
    fn: Callable[[Float64[np.ndarray, " time"]], Float[np.ndarray, " time"]], n: int, phase: float
) -> Callable[[], pa.Array]:
    """Build a deterministic lazy loader for a closed-form wave.

    The connector uses this loader for the long series that the writer splits into chunks.

    Args:
        fn: The wave function to apply to the angular time base, for example ``np.sin``.
        n: The number of samples.
        phase: The phase offset in radians.

    Returns:
        A loader with no arguments. The loader returns the wave as a float32 Arrow array.
    """
    return lambda: pa.array(_wave_values(fn, n, phase))


class HelloWorldConnector(BaseConnector[HelloWorldRecording]):
    """A deterministic, offline demo connector for the ``timenet/hello-world`` dataset."""

    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[HelloWorldRecording]:  # noqa: ARG002, PLR6301 (override: the data is synthetic, so this method needs no cache)
        """Return deterministic recording descriptions.

        This method uses no network and does not use ``cache_dir``.

        Args:
            cache_dir: Not used. The data is synthetic.

        Returns:
            One short recording and one longer recording. The writer splits the longer recording into
            chunks under a small chunk cap.
        """
        return [HelloWorldRecording(index=0, n_values=16), HelloWorldRecording(index=1, n_values=512)]

    def convert(self, raw_refs: list[HelloWorldRecording]) -> TimeFDataset:
        """Build the complete dataset from the recording descriptions.

        The dataset includes every TimeF feature.

        Args:
            raw_refs: The recordings from :meth:`download`.

        Returns:
            The populated :class:`~timenet.dataset.TimeFDataset`.
        """
        dataset = TimeFDataset(metadata=self.metadata())
        short, long = raw_refs[0], raw_refs[1]

        # A series shared across two records. This uses the dedupe-by-id path.
        shared = TimeSeries.from_values(
            _wave_values(np.sin, short.n_values, phase=0.0),
            spec=_SINE,
            signal="a",
            time_axis=_AXIS,
            source_id="rec-0",
            time_series_id="ts-shared",
        )
        # An annotation shared across two records. This uses the dedupe-by-id path.
        cohort = Annotation(key="cohort", value="A", id="cohort-shared")

        # Record 0: the full recording, with two modalities, all annotation shapes, and a task chain.
        cosine = TimeSeries.from_values(
            _wave_values(np.cos, short.n_values, phase=0.0),
            spec=_COSINE,
            signal="b",
            time_axis=_AXIS,
            source_id="rec-0",
            time_series_id="ts-cos-0",
        )
        record0 = dataset.add_record(time_series=(shared, cosine), subject_ids=("subj-0",), record_id="record-0")
        # These annotations have names. The localization task below can reference them by id instead
        # of repeating the literal values.
        stimulus = Annotation(key="stimulus", span=TimePoint.seconds(0.5), id="stim-0")
        artifact = Annotation(
            key="artifact",
            span=TimeInterval.seconds(0.0, 0.25, time_series_ids=(shared.time_series_id,)),
            id="art-0",
        )
        record0.add_annotations(
            [
                Annotation(key="age", value=64, unit="years", id="age-0"),
                cohort,
                stimulus,
                artifact,
            ]
        )
        classification = ClassificationTask(target="normal", id="task-cls-0")
        dataset.add_tasks(
            record0,
            [
                classification,
                AnswerTask(
                    prompt="What rhythm?",
                    target="Normal.",
                    # Any task can carry a chain of thought. An answer task with a chain of thought is
                    # the old reasoning task.
                    rationale="The peaks repeat once per cycle at a constant interval.",
                    # The cohort annotation gives context to the model. The model does not need to
                    # produce this annotation.
                    input_annotation_ids=(cohort.id,),
                    from_tasks=(classification,),
                    id="task-answer-0",
                ),
                ScalarPredictionTask(target=60.0, unit="bpm", target_name="mean_rate", id="task-scalar-0"),
                # Localization works backward from a normal task. The query is the input, and the
                # regions are the output. Here, the task stores the answer by reference, so the target
                # is the two temporal annotations above.
                TemporalLocalizationTask(
                    prompt="Locate the stimulus and the artifact.",
                    mode=LocalizationMode.SPARSE,
                    target_annotation_ids=(stimulus.id, artifact.id),
                    id="task-localize-0",
                ),
            ],
        )

        # Record 1: this reuses the shared series and adds a longer series. The writer tests split the
        # longer series into chunks under a small chunk cap.
        long_series = TimeSeries(

"""A synthetic, offline connector that tests every TimeF feature.

``HelloWorldConnector`` needs no network. It creates a fully deterministic dataset. The writer and
reader test suites use this dataset as a fixture for round-trip tests. The connector covers two
modalities, a shared data source, a series shared across records, and a windowed record. It also
covers a longer series. The writer tests split this longer series into chunks under a small chunk
cap. The connector covers all three annotation shapes, including one shared across records, and a
task chain.

from dataclasses import dataclass

import pyarrow as pa

from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries
from timenet.dataset.axis import RegularAxis
from timenet.types import (
    Annotation,
    AnswerTask,
    ClassificationTask,
    DataSource,
    LocalizationMode,
    ScalarPredictionTask,
    TemporalLocalizationTask,
    TimeInterval,
    TimePoint,
    TimeSeriesSpec,
    ureg,
)


_SAMPLING_RATE_HZ = 16.0
_AXIS = RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(16)
_SOURCE = DataSource(data_source_type="synthetic", name="Synthetic Generator", provider="TimeNet")
_SINE = TimeSeriesSpec(
    spec_type="sine",
    name="Sine",
    unit_value=ureg.dimensionless,
    data_source=_SOURCE,
)
_COSINE = TimeSeriesSpec(
    spec_type="cosine",
    name="Cosine",
    unit_value=ureg.dimensionless,
    data_source=_SOURCE,
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class HelloWorldRecording:
    """A lightweight, deterministic description of one synthetic recording."""

    index: int
    n_values: int


def _wave_values(
    fn: Callable[[Float64[np.ndarray, " time"]], Float[np.ndarray, " time"]], n: int, phase: float
) -> Float[np.ndarray, " time"]:
    """Compute a closed-form wave as an array.

    The function does not use a random number generator or perform I/O.

    Args:
        fn: The wave function to apply to the angular time base, for example ``np.sin``.
        n: The number of samples.
        phase: The phase offset in radians.

    Returns:
        The wave values as a float32 ``np.ndarray``.
    """
    t = np.arange(n, dtype=np.float64) / _SAMPLING_RATE_HZ
    return fn(2.0 * np.pi * t + phase).astype(np.float32)


def _wave(
    fn: Callable[[Float64[np.ndarray, " time"]], Float[np.ndarray, " time"]], n: int, phase: float
) -> Callable[[], pa.Array]:
    """Build a deterministic lazy loader for a closed-form wave.

    The connector uses this loader for the long series that the writer splits into chunks.

    Args:
        fn: The wave function to apply to the angular time base, for example ``np.sin``.
        n: The number of samples.
        phase: The phase offset in radians.

    Returns:
        A loader with no arguments. The loader returns the wave as a float32 Arrow array.
    """
    return lambda: pa.array(_wave_values(fn, n, phase))

    """A deterministic, offline demo connector for the ``timenet/hello-world`` dataset."""

    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[HelloWorldRecording]:  # noqa: ARG002, PLR6301 (override: the data is synthetic, so this method needs no cache)

        Args:

        Returns:

            chunks under a small chunk cap.
        """

        """Build the complete dataset from the recording descriptions.

            raw_refs: The recordings from :meth:`download`.

        Returns:

        dataset = TimeFDataset(metadata=self.metadata())

        shared = TimeSeries.from_values(
            _wave_values(np.sin, short.n_values, phase=0.0),

            source_id="rec-0",
            time_series_id="ts-cos-0",

        artifact = Annotation(
            key="artifact",
            span=TimeInterval.seconds(0.0, 0.25, time_series_ids=(shared.time_series_id,)),
            id="art-0",
        )
        record0.add_annotations(
            [
                Annotation(key="age", value=64, unit="years", id="age-0"),
                cohort,
                stimulus,
                artifact,
            ]
        )
        classification = ClassificationTask(target="normal", id="task-cls-0")
        dataset.add_tasks(
            record0,
            [
                classification,
                AnswerTask(
                    prompt="What rhythm?",
                    target="Normal.",
                    # Any task can carry a chain of thought. An answer task with a chain of thought is
                    # the old reasoning task.
                    rationale="The peaks repeat once per cycle at a constant interval.",
                    # The cohort annotation gives context to the model. The model does not need to

                # is the two temporal annotations above.

                    id="task-localize-0",
                ),
            ],
        )

        # Record 1: this reuses the shared series and adds a longer series. The writer tests split the
        # longer series into chunks under a small chunk cap.

            spec=_SINE,
            signal="a",
            time_axis=_AXIS,

            spec=_SINE,

            time_axis=_AXIS.at_index(window_start),
            source_id="rec-0",
            time_series_id="ts-window-2",
        )
        record2 = dataset.add_record(time_series=(window,), subject_ids=("subj-0",), record_id="record-2")
        # A scope narrows the input to a region. This task has the same task type as the whole-record
        # label above, but it supplies the window. Span times use the source recording timeline, so

content.text:
All three checked. The compatibility requirement makes the plan cheaper, not harder.

## Most recent data

The August 2026 file spans the first to the last day of that month, so the data ends twelve days ago. Coverage runs from July 2024 across twenty-six monthly files.

| Newest month | Rows | Distinct stations |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-08 | 14.3M | 5,203 |

## The T+00:00 point

Your instinct is right that it reads wrong, but a date is not the fix. The board's idea parser requires a `T` followed by a sign and `HH:MM`. A calendar date fails the match, and the entry then vanishes from the dashboard silently rather than erroring. Separately, the board's own timestamp helper returns exactly the string `T+00:00` when the build start is unset, so the file already matches what its API would have written today. The format does accept a minus sign, so the honest label for pre-event ideas is a negative offset once you know the start time. I rewrote the note in the file to say that.

## OpenTSLM compatibility

Verified against their code, not the paper. The connector contract is two methods and a card: fetch raw references, convert them to a dataset, ship a yaml file, end the module by assigning your class. No constructor arguments.

- **Half the connector already exists.** There is a Hugging Face base connector where you set the repo id and implement only the conversion step. Your dataset is on the Hub, so that path fits.
- **One trap in it.** The inherited download returns one dictionary per row across the whole repo. At 226 million rows that is unusable, so override it to pull only the monthly files you selected.
- **Your three questions map onto their task types directly.** Scalar prediction for the six-hour mean, classification for the comparison and the peak hour. Every task carries a rationale field, so chain of thought is first-class rather than something you bolt on.
- **The text baseline is already written.** Their question-answering base class has a string-formatting path that serialises the same series into the prompt. The comparison I called the headline costs you no code.
- **They ship an agent skill for building connectors.** Point a coding agent at it instead of reverse-engineering the contract.

Two things the deck settles. Compute is no longer a blocker, since each team gets a Nebius voucher plus training access, so I marked that idea discarded. The submission list explicitly accepts a checkpoint or an adapter, which supports keeping the base model frozen.

One real gap. The deck puts identifying a target user and problem as step one, and a useful problem heads the strong-project list. The train direction still has no named user. That needs an answer before the pitch, not after.

Checked: all seventeen ideas parse through the board's own parser, and the seventeen board tests pass. Nothing committed.

result: verified OpenTSLM and TimeNet compatibility against their source, found the Hugging Face connector base and the free text baseline both cut work, flagged that the inherited row-streaming download breaks at 226M rows, confirmed data runs through August 2026, and kept T+00:00 because the board regex rejects calendar dates

content.content:
# Feature: training-jobs

Submit, track, and cancel GPU training runs on **Nebius Serverless AI jobs**
from this backend. A job is a container on a fresh GPU VM: you give it an
image, a command, a platform/preset, and a timeout; Nebius bills the VM while
it runs and releases everything when the container exits.

- `nebius/auth.js`   – access tokens (static token, service-account JWT, or CLI)
- `nebius/client.js` – REST client for `ai/v1/jobs` (+ `iam/v1/profiles`, `vpc/v1/subnets`)
- `nebius/spec.js`   – validated `CreateJobRequest` builder, platform catalog, cost estimate
- `routes/`          – HTTP endpoints under `/api/training/*`
- `cli.js`           – terminal front-end over the same service (`npm run train -- ...`)
- `examples/`        – nvidia-smi check, a distilgpt2 fine-tune, a bring-your-own-image spec

Zero npm dependencies: Node ≥ 22 built-ins only (fetch, crypto, http).

## 0. Team access (once per teammate)

Everyone submits jobs against the same Nebius project, so they need to be a
member of it. The account owner does this in https://console.nebius.com:
**Administration → IAM → Groups → editors → Add member** (invite by email).
Each teammate then does section 1 on their own machine. Nothing secret lives
in git: `.env`, `secrets/` and `*.pem` are ignored, so every person keeps
their own login. A shared service-account key is only for a deployed server.

## 1. One-time setup (10 minutes)

### a. Nebius CLI (already installed on this Mac at `~/.nebius/bin/nebius`)

```bash
curl -sSL https://storage.eu-north1.nebius.cloud/cli/install.sh | bash   # if missing
exec -l $SHELL                                                            # picks up PATH
nebius profile create --profile default \
  --endpoint api.nebius.cloud --federation-endpoint auth.nebius.com \
  --parent-id <project_ID>          # opens the browser to log in
nebius profile list                 # sanity check
```

Project ID: **Administration → Projects** in https://console.nebius.com, or
`nebius iam v2 project list --parent-id <tenant_ID>`. It looks like `project-e00…`.

### b. Quota

**Administration → Limits → Quotas → Compute → Number of virtual machines**
must be ≥ 1, and the GPU platform you want (L40S / H100 …) must have a non-zero
quota. Request an increase in the console if not; jobs fail with
`NotEnoughResources` otherwise.

### c. Backend env

```bash
cp app/backend/.env.example app/backend/.env
# set NEBIUS_PROJECT_ID; leave NEBIUS_SUBNET_ID blank for now
cd app/backend && npm run train -- doctor
```

`doctor` authenticates, prints who you are, lists subnets, and tells you the
`NEBIUS_SUBNET_ID` to paste into `.env` if the project has one subnet.

### d. Auth: pick one

| Mode | When | Setup |
|---|---|---|
| CLI profile (default) | laptop, hackathon | nothing beyond `nebius profile create`; the backend shells out to `nebius iam get-access-token` |
| `NEBIUS_ACCESS_TOKEN` | CI, a teammate's machine, 12 h | `nebius iam get-access-token` and paste into `.env` |
| Service account | deployed backend | see below |

Service account (non-interactive, long-lived):

```bash
export SA_ID=$(nebius iam service-account create --name backend-trainer --format jsonpath='{.metadata.id}')
# give it editor rights: Administration → IAM → Groups → editors → add member $SA_ID  (or nebius iam group-membership create ...)
openssl genrsa -out app/backend/secrets/nebius-sa.pem 4096
openssl rsa -in app/backend/secrets/nebius-sa.pem -pubout -out /tmp/nebius-sa.pub.pem
nebius iam auth-public-key create --account-service-account-id $SA_ID --data "$(cat /tmp/nebius-sa.pub.pem)"
# key ID: console → IAM → Service accounts → backend-trainer → Authorized keys
```

Then in `.env`: `NEBIUS_SA_ID`, `NEBIUS_SA_KEY_ID`, `NEBIUS_SA_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE=./secrets/nebius-sa.pem`.
`secrets/` and `*.pem` are git-ignored.

## 2. Run it

### Smoke test (Nebius's own quick start: nvidia-smi on 1× L40S, ~$0.10)

```bash
cd app/backend
npm run train -- smoke
```

Submits, polls every 15 s through `PROVISIONING → STARTING → IMAGE_PULLING →
RUNNING → COMPLETED`, then prints the last 100 log lines (the `nvidia-smi`
table). Takes 3–6 minutes end to end. Exit code 0 means the whole path works.

### Train a script

```bash
npm run train -- submit \
  --name distilgpt2-run1 \
  --script src/features/training-jobs/examples/train.py \
  --requirements src/features/training-jobs/examples/requirements.txt \
  --platform gpu-l40s-a --preset 1gpu-8vcpu-32gb --timeout 1h \
  --env HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \
  --wait \
  -- --epochs 1 --max-steps 50
```

What happens: the script and requirements are **injected** into the container
at `/workspace/` (limit 64 KiB per file), a generated `run.sh` runs
`pip install -r requirements.txt && python train.py …`, and the job is created.
Without `--wait` the command returns immediately with the job ID.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--script`, `--requirements` | local files to inject |
| `--platform`, `--preset` | see `npm run train -- catalog` |
| `--timeout` | `1h`…`168h`; the job is killed and billed up to this |
| `--image` | default `pytorch/pytorch:2.7.1-cuda12.8-cudnn9-runtime` |
| `--env K=V` (repeatable) | env vars for the container |
| `--volume SRC:/path[:ro]` (repeatable) | mount a Nebius bucket/filesystem or `s3://bucket` |

######## README ######## # OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data [![PyPI - Version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/opentslm)](https://pypi.org/project/opentslm) [![DOI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DOI-10.48550/arXiv.2510.02410-blue.svg)](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2510.02410) [![Static Analysis](https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/OpenTSLM/actions/workflows/static-analysis.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SchmiedmayerLab/OpenTSLM/actions/workflows/static-analysis.yml) Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting multimodal data (e.g., images, audio, text), often surpassing specialized models. In medicine, they hold particular promise for synthesizing large volumes of clinical information into actionable insights and patient-facing digital health applications. Yet, a major limitation remains their inability to handle time series data. To overcome this gap, we present OpenTSLM, a family of Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) created by integrating time series as a native modality to pretrained Large Language Models, enabling natural-language prompting and reasoning over multiple time series of any length [...] **[🔗 Read the full paper](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2510.02410)**

## Examples OpenTSLM models can reason over multiple time series of any length at once, generating findings, captions, and rationales in natural language. We tested these models across a wide range of tasks spanning Human Activity Recognition (HAR) from 3-axis acceleration data, sleep staging from EEG readings, 12-lead ECG question answering, and time series captioning. Some examples are shown below, more are available in the paper.

## Installation ```bash pip install opentslm ``` ## LLM Setup OpenTSLM is designed to work with Llama and Gemma models, with Llama 3.2 1B as the default. These models are stored in Hugging Face repositories which may require access permissions. Follow these steps to gain access and download: 1. **Request Access (for Llama models)** Visit the Llama model repository (e.g., https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B) or Gemma models repository (https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-3-270m) and request access from Meta. 2. **Authenticate with Hugging Face** Log in to your Hugging Face account and configure the CLI: ```bash huggingface-cli login ``` 3. **Create an API Token** - Go to your Hugging Face settings: https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens - Generate a new token with `read` scope. - Copy the token for CLI login. ### Supported Models OpenTSLM has been tested and works with the following models: **Llama Models:** - **meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B** (default) - **meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B** **Gemma Models:** - **google/gemma-3-270m** - **google/gemma-3-1b-pt** Other variants may work but have not been extensively tested. ## 🤗 Quickstart with pretrained models on HuggingFace A factory class called `OpenTSLM` for easily loading pre-trained models from Hugging Face Hub. The `load_pretrained` method automatically detects the model type and returns the appropriate model instance. There are [demo scripts](demo/huggingface/) available which use the following minimal code. If you want to create your own applications, create a new file in **this repo folder** and use the following code as start: ```python from opentslm import OpenTSLM from opentslm.time_series_datasets.TSQADataset import TSQADataset from opentslm.time_series_datasets.util import extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate from torch.utils.data import DataLoader from opentslm.model_config import PATCH_SIZE REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp" # Use CPU or CUDA for inference. MPS does NOT work for pretrained HF checkpoints. model = OpenTSLM.load_pretrained(REPO_ID, device="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") test_dataset = TSQADataset("test", EOS_TOKEN=model.get_eos_token()) test_loader = DataLoader( test_dataset, shuffle=False, batch_size=1, collate_fn=lambda batch: extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate( batch, patch_size=PATCH_SIZE ), ) for i, batch in enumerate(test_loader): predictions = model.generate(batch, max_new_tokens=200) for sample, pred in zip(batch, predictions): print("Question:", sample.get("pre_prompt", "N/A")) print("Answer:", sample.get("answer", "N/A")) print("Output:", pred) if i >= 4: break ``` ## Building and finetuning your own models To run the demos and use finetuning scripts **clone the repository** and set up all dependencies. We recommend using [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) to set up the environment, but you can also use pip: ```bash git clone https://github.com/OpenTSLM/OpenTSLM.git # uv environment management (recommended). Installs uv if it does not exist and creates the virtual environment command uv > /dev/null || curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh uv sync --all-groups source .venv/bin/activate # or alternatively install via pip: pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ### HuggingFace Demo Scripts We provide ready-to-use demo scripts in the `demo/huggingface/` directory that demonstrate how to load pretrained models from HuggingFace Hub and run inference on the evaluation sets for each task: - **`01_test_hf_tsqa.py`** - Test TSQA (Time Series Question Answering) models - **`02_test_hf_m4.py`** - Test M4 (Time Series Captioning) models - **`03_test_hf_har_cot.py`** - Test HAR CoT (Human Activity Recognition Chain-of-Thought) models - **`04_test_hf_sleep_cot.py`** - Test Sleep CoT (Sleep Stage Classification) models Shell cwd was reset to /Users/jonasstenglein/OtherProjects/EHL_Zurich/temporal_ai_error404.ai

- **`05_test_hf_ecg_qa_cot.py`** - Test ECG QA CoT (ECG Question Answering) models

Each script:

4. Prints model outputs with sample information

**Note:** The scripts above use the OpenTSLM-SP models except for ECG-QA, as they require less VRAM and should run on most hardware. Change the model checkpoints as needed in each file. 

**Usage:**

```bash
# Run any of the demo scripts
python demo/huggingface/01_test_hf_tsqa.py
python demo/huggingface/02_test_hf_m4.py
python demo/huggingface/03_test_hf_har_cot.py
python demo/huggingface/04_test_hf_sleep_cot.py
python demo/huggingface/05_test_hf_ecg_qa_cot.py
```

**Customizing the model:**

Edit the `REPO_ID` variable at the top of each script to test different model variants. For example:

```python
# In 01_test_hf_tsqa.py
REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp"  # Soft Prompt model
# or
REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-flamingo"  # Flamingo model
```

**Available models on HuggingFace:**

All pretrained models are available under the `OpenTSLM` organization on HuggingFace Hub. Model names follow the pattern:
- `OpenTSLM/{base_model}-{dataset}-{model_type}`
   - `base_model`: `llama-3.2-1b`, `llama-3.2-3b`, `gemma-3-1b-pt`, `gemma-3-270m`
   - `dataset`: `tsqa`, `m4`, `har`, `sleep`, `ecg`
   - `model_type`: `sp` (Soft Prompt) or `flamingo` (Flamingo)

Example: `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-ecg-flamingo`

## Training: Multi-stage training (Curriculum)

OpenTSLM uses curriculum learning with progressive training stages:

### Training Stages

1. **Stage 1 (MCQ)**: Multiple choice questions on time series data (TSQA dataset)
2. **Stage 2 (Captioning)**: Generate detailed captions for time series (M4 dataset)
3. **Stage 3 (CoT)**: Chain-of-thought reasoning on human activity recognition (HAR dataset)
4. **Stage 4 (Sleep CoT)**: Chain-of-thought reasoning on sleep stage classification (SleepEDF dataset)
5. **Stage 5 (ECG CoT)**: Chain-of-thought reasoning on ECG question answering (ECG QA dataset)

> **⚠️ MPS/CUDA Compatibility Warning:**
>
> If you are using Apple's MPS (Metal Performance Shaders) backend (e.g., on Mac with Apple Silicon), you may encounter issues with training or inference. **Checkpoints trained with CUDA (NVIDIA GPUs) may not yield good results or may not be fully compatible when loaded and run on MPS.** For best results, use the same device type (CUDA or MPS) for both training and inference. CUDA is preferred in general.

### Quick Start

```bash
# Run full curriculum with OpenTSLMFlamingo
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMSP

# Run full curriculum with OpenTSLMSP
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo

# Run specific stages
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage1_mcq
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage2_captioning
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage3_cot
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage4_sleep_cot
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage5_ecg_cot

# Run multiple stages
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage1_mcq stage2_captioning stage3_cot

# Specify device
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --device cuda

# Use different models
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --llm_id meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --llm_id google/gemma-3-270m

# Run only evaluation
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --eval_only
```

```bash
python demo/huggingface/05_test_hf_ecg_qa_cot.py
```

**Customizing the model:**

Edit the `REPO_ID` variable at the top of each script to test different model variants. For example:

```python
# In 01_test_hf_tsqa.py
REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-sp"  # Soft Prompt model
# or
REPO_ID = "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-tsqa-flamingo"  # Flamingo model
```

**Available models on HuggingFace:**

All pretrained models are available under the `OpenTSLM` organization on HuggingFace Hub. Model names follow the pattern:
- `OpenTSLM/{base_model}-{dataset}-{model_type}`
   - `base_model`: `llama-3.2-1b`, `llama-3.2-3b`, `gemma-3-1b-pt`, `gemma-3-270m`
   - `dataset`: `tsqa`, `m4`, `har`, `sleep`, `ecg`
   - `model_type`: `sp` (Soft Prompt) or `flamingo` (Flamingo)

Example: `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-1b-ecg-flamingo`

## Training: Multi-stage training (Curriculum)

OpenTSLM uses curriculum learning with progressive training stages:

### Training Stages

1. **Stage 1 (MCQ)**: Multiple choice questions on time series data (TSQA dataset)
2. **Stage 2 (Captioning)**: Generate detailed captions for time series (M4 dataset)
3. **Stage 3 (CoT)**: Chain-of-thought reasoning on human activity recognition (HAR dataset)
4. **Stage 4 (Sleep CoT)**: Chain-of-thought reasoning on sleep stage classification (SleepEDF dataset)
5. **Stage 5 (ECG CoT)**: Chain-of-thought reasoning on ECG question answering (ECG QA dataset)

> **⚠️ MPS/CUDA Compatibility Warning:**
>
> If you are using Apple's MPS (Metal Performance Shaders) backend (e.g., on Mac with Apple Silicon), you may encounter issues with training or inference. **Checkpoints trained with CUDA (NVIDIA GPUs) may not yield good results or may not be fully compatible when loaded and run on MPS.** For best results, use the same device type (CUDA or MPS) for both training and inference. CUDA is preferred in general.

### Quick Start

```bash
# Run full curriculum with OpenTSLMFlamingo
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMSP

# Run full curriculum with OpenTSLMSP
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo

# Run specific stages
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage1_mcq
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage2_captioning
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage3_cot
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage4_sleep_cot
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage5_ecg_cot

# Run multiple stages
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --stages stage1_mcq stage2_captioning stage3_cot

# Specify device
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --device cuda

# Use different models
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --llm_id meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --llm_id google/gemma-3-270m

# Run only evaluation
python curriculum_learning.py --model OpenTSLMFlamingo --eval_only
```

content.text:
Connector first is right, and the research turned up a gap that makes it more valuable than I thought.

## The gap worth building

OpenTSLM does not depend on TimeNet. Its requirements list has no timenet entry, and its dataset classes each load their own source directly. So the two halves of their own stack are not wired together: a TimeF dataset cannot currently feed OpenTSLM training.

That missing piece is about eighty lines and it maps cleanly, because their task objects already carry a prompt, a target, and a rationale, which is exactly what the training base class wants as pre-prompt, answer, and chain of thought. Building a generic bridge from any TimeF dataset to an OpenTSLM training set is reusable by every other team and by the organizers, which is precisely what the deck calls especially valuable. So the order becomes connector, bridge, training, and the bridge is the part judges have not seen before.

## Proving it works

The fastest independent check needs none of our code. The merged backend has a smoke command that submits a trivial GPU job and prints the result, so it validates the whole compute path on its own.

| Check | Time | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Nebius smoke job | 3 to 6 min | about $0.10 |
| One-time Nebius setup before it | about 10 min | none |

On your hour question, honestly: a throwaway run in roughly an hour is achievable, since the data query is already proven and there is a built-in sample cap for quick experiments. A run worth showing is about five hours from now, which still leaves fifteen hours before the submit target.

Two constraints shape the packaging. The job runner injects only a script and a requirements file, capped at 64 KiB each, so the container has to clone OpenTSLM and fetch our prepared data from somewhere remote rather than receiving it. And the training entry point validates stage names against a fixed list, so our data arrives as a new stage in a fork, not a flag.

On the base model, pick the smallest Gemma. Both it and Llama are gated, but Meta approval can take hours while the Google terms usually clear immediately, and at 270M parameters it also trains fastest.

## What I need from you

1. **A Hugging Face token with read scope**, and someone accepting the Gemma terms. This is the single longest pole if it slips.
2. **Nebius access.** The CLI is not installed on this machine and no environment file exists, so either you set it up or whoever wrote that backend runs the jobs. I also need the project identifier and confirmation that GPU quota is above zero.
3. **An owner for the code directories.** The owners file is empty and the repo rules stop me editing under the app tree without an assignment.
4. **The target user.** Still unanswered, and it is the first line of the rubric.
5. **Where the prepared dataset lives** so the container can pull it, either a dataset repo or a bucket.

I can start the data slice and draft the connector against the selection I proposed without any of these. Only item three actually blocks me from writing code.

"""Turn the hourly station table into fixed windows with deterministic targets.

The unit of analysis is one station's hourly delay curve, not one train run: a
run visits too few stops, too irregularly, for a patch encoder to beat a plain
text baseline. Every target here is computed from the horizon by a function,
never written by hand, so the labels stay objective.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np

CONTEXT_HOURS = 168  # one week
HORIZON_HOURS = 24
STRIDE_HOURS = 24
FORECAST_HOURS = 6
MAX_IMPUTED_FRACTION = 0.10

CHANNELS = ("mean_delay", "cancel_rate", "trains")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Window:
    """One context window plus the targets derived from the horizon after it."""

    station: str
    start_index: int
    context: dict[str, np.ndarray]
    imputed_fraction: float
    next_6h_mean_delay: float
    worse_than_context: bool
    peak_hour_of_next_day: int
    context_mean_delay: float
    horizon_mean_delay: float
    hour_of_day_at_start: int

"""Build a TimeF dataset of German rail delay from the hourly station table."""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
from fractions import Fraction

import numpy as np

from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries
from timenet.dataset.axis import RegularAxis
from timenet.types import (
    Annotation,
    ClassificationTask,
    DataSource,
    DatasetMetadata,
    ScalarPredictionTask,
    TimeSeriesSpec,
    ureg,
)

from windows import CHANNELS, CONTEXT_HOURS, build_windows, impute
from windows import rationale_for_comparison, rationale_for_forecast, rationale_for_peak

HOURLY = RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1, 3600))
SOURCE = DataSource(
    data_source_type="operational-record",
    name="Deutsche Bahn timetable scrape",
    provider="piebro/deutsche-bahn-data",
)
SPECS = {
    "mean_delay": TimeSeriesSpec(
        spec_type="delay", name="Mean delay", unit_value=ureg.minute, data_source=SOURCE
    ),
    "cancel_rate": TimeSeriesSpec(
        spec_type="cancellation-rate",
        name="Cancellation rate",
        unit_value=ureg.dimensionless,
        data_source=SOURCE,
    ),
    "trains": TimeSeriesSpec(
        spec_type="throughput", name="Trains per hour", unit_value=ureg.dimensionless, data_source=SOURCE
    ),
}


def metadata() -> DatasetMetadata:
    """Return the dataset card for this build."""
    return DatasetMetadata(
        dataset_id="error404/db-delay-hourly",
        dataset_version="0.1.0",
        name="German rail hourly station delay",
        description=(
            "Hourly mean delay, cancellation rate and train count per German station, "
            "windowed into one-week contexts with forecast, comparison and peak-hour targets."
        ),
        license="CC-BY-4.0",
        domains=("transport",),
        tags=("rail", "delay", "forecasting", "qa"),
        source_url="https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data",
    )


def grids_from_duckdb(con, month_start: dt.datetime, n_hours: int):
    """Read the hourly table and lay each station out on a complete hourly grid.

    Args:
        con: An open DuckDB connection holding the ``hourly`` table.
        month_start: The first hour of the month.
        n_hours: How many hours the month spans.

    Yields:
        One ``(station, grid, present)`` triple per station.
    """
    rows = con.execute(
        "SELECT station_name, hour, mean_delay, cancel_rate, trains FROM hourly ORDER BY 1, 2"
    ).fetchall()
    by_station: dict[str, list] = {}
    for station, hour, *values in rows:
        by_station.setdefault(station, []).append((hour, values))
    for station, entries in by_station.items():
        grid = {name: np.zeros(n_hours, dtype=np.float64) for name in CHANNELS}
        present = np.zeros(n_hours, dtype=bool)
        for hour, values in entries:
            index = int((hour - month_start).total_seconds() // 3600)
            if not 0 <= index < n_hours:
                continue
            present[index] = True
            for name, value in zip(CHANNELS, values, strict=True):
                grid[name][index] = value
        filled = {
            name: impute(grid[name], present, "zero" if name == "trains" else "interpolate")
            for name in CHANNELS
        }
        yield station, filled, present


def build(con, month_start: dt.datetime, n_hours: int) -> TimeFDataset:
    """Convert the hourly table into a TimeF dataset with one record per window."""
    dataset = TimeFDataset(metadata=metadata())
    for station, grid, present in grids_from_duckdb(con, month_start, n_hours):
        for window in build_windows(station, grid, present):
            slug = f"{station.replace(' ', '-').lower()}-{window.start_index:04d}"
            series = tuple(
                TimeSeries.from_values(
                    window.context[name].astype(np.float32),
                    spec=SPECS[name],
                    signal=name,
                    time_axis=HOURLY,
                    source_id=station,
                    time_series_id=f"{slug}-{name}",
                )
                for name in CHANNELS
            )
            record = dataset.add_record(
                time_series=series,
                subject_ids=(station,),
                record_id=slug,
                start_time=month_start + dt.timedelta(hours=window.start_index),
            )
            record.add_annotations(
                [
                    Annotation(key="station", value=station, id=f"{slug}-station"),
                    Annotation(key="imputed_fraction", value=round(window.imputed_fraction, 4), id=f"{slug}-imp"),
                    Annotation(key="context_hours", value=CONTEXT_HOURS, id=f"{slug}-ctx"),
                ]
            )
            dataset.add_tasks(
                record,
                [
                    ScalarPredictionTask(
                        prompt=f"What is the mean delay in minutes at {station} over the next six hours?",
                        target=round(window.next_6h_mean_delay, 3),
                        unit="minute",
                        target_name="next_6h_mean_delay",
                        rationale=rationale_for_forecast(window),
                        id=f"{slug}-forecast",
                    ),
                    ClassificationTask(
                        prompt=f"Will the next day at {station} be worse than the past week's average?",
                        target="worse" if window.worse_than_context else "not_worse",
                        target_schema="worse|not_worse",
                        rationale=rationale_for_comparison(window),
                        id=f"{slug}-comparison",
                    ),
                    ClassificationTask(
                        prompt=f"At which hour of the coming day does delay peak at {station}?",
                        target=f"{window.peak_hour_of_next_day:02d}",
                        target_schema="00..23",
                        rationale=rationale_for_peak(window),
                        id=f"{slug}-peak",
                    ),
                ],
            )
    return dataset
