- **Where every number in the label comes from**, which is the part that answers "how does the annotation work". It also states the honest cost: only three sentence shapes across 7,338 examples.
- **The six pipeline stages**, with the bridge stage highlighted because it did not exist upstream.
- **Proof the signal is real**, as delay by hour of day. It peaks at 11.4 minutes after midnight and collapses to 1.9 at six in the morning when the timetable restarts.
- **The four evaluation cells** and why only one of them counts.
- **The first run's numbers, unvarnished.** Forecast roughly level with baseline, comparison below majority, peak-hour failing.
- **A two-column verdict.** Five things we have that others will not, five things that are genuinely weak.
- **Seven ranked next steps** with time estimates and, where obvious, a name.

The recommendation it argues: pursue it, on the strength of the pipeline rather than the current score. The two highest-value moves are naming a target user, which needs a person rather than a coder, and accepting the Gemma licence so we can start from a pretrained encoder instead of random weights.

Nothing was committed or pushed. The page is built from a file in the scratch directory, so tell me what to change and I will republish to the same link.

02  What the model receives

Channels, points, and how numbers become tokens

  • Channel

    One measurement tracked over time. We use three, recorded at the same hours and running in parallel: how late trains were, what share was cancelled, and how many passed through.

  • Point

    One hour. A point is the whole station's traffic in that hour boiled down to one number per channel.

  • Window

    168 points, because 24 hours times 7 days is a week. Long enough to contain both the daily rhythm and the weekday-weekend difference.

Normalizing, concretely

Each channel is rescaled by subtracting its own mean and dividing by its own standard deviation. For the delay channel of the example above, whose week averaged 2.012 minutes with a spread of 1.508:

HourRaw delayArithmeticWhat the model sees
02.00 min(2.00 − 2.012) ÷ 1.508−0.008
11.06 min(1.06 − 2.012) ÷ 1.508−0.630
20.85 min(0.85 − 2.012) ÷ 1.508−0.770
30.64 min(0.64 − 2.012) ÷ 1.508−0.911

Read the last column as distance from a typical hour that week. Hour 1 sat 0.63 standard deviations below normal.

Why bother

The three channels live on wildly different scales, and without rescaling the model would treat train counts as the most important simply because their numbers are biggest.

ChannelRaw rangeAfter normalizing
Mean delay0 to 11.33 min−1.33 to 6.18
Cancellation rate0 to 0.44−0.97 to 5.50
Trains per hour0 to 94−2.24 to 1.02

Afterwards all three sit in a comparable band, so the encoder weighs shape rather than magnitude. Note the delay channel still reaches 6.18. That is a real spike six standard deviations above its own normal, and it stays visible as a spike rather than being flattened away.

The catch: normalizing throws away the absolute level, so the numbers alone can no longer tell you anything is measured in minutes. The question asks for minutes. That is why each series is introduced in the prompt with its own mean and standard deviation, letting the model convert back. It is also the convention OpenTSLM's own reasoning datasets use, so we match it rather than inventing our own.

From numbers to tokens

A language model consumes vectors, not floats. Each channel is cut into four-hour patches, each patch is encoded, and the result is projected into the same space the model's word embeddings live in. The series then sits inside the prompt as if it were text.

Input168 × 3 Hourly points, three channels, normalized.
Patch42 patches Cut into four-hour blocks. A convolution turns each block into one vector.
Encode128 dims A transformer reads the patch sequence, so a patch is understood in the context of the week around it.
Project896 dims A learned layer maps each vector into the language model's own embedding width.
Prompt126 vectors Three channels of 42, slotted between the words of the question.

Only the encoder and the projector are trained from scratch, which is 11 million parameters. The language model itself is adapted lightly with LoRA. That is the whole trick behind a time-series language model: teach a small translator to speak the frozen model's language, rather than retraining the model.

""" anchor = '
\n

03  How the labels are made

' assert anchor in s s = s.replace(anchor, section.strip() + "\n\n" + anchor, 1) open(p, "w").write(s) print("sections now:", s.count("
")) PY

It did not, so I added it. Same link, now version 2: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e5c9eb52-c83b-446b-9fef-9a39c59c6878**

The new section sits second, right after the worked example, and covers four things the page was missing.

**Plain definitions** of channel, point and window, so a reader who has never touched time-series data knows what 168 by 3 means before any arithmetic appears.

**Normalizing shown as arithmetic, not described.** A table walks the first four hours from raw minutes through the subtraction and division to the number the model actually receives, using the real mean of 2.012 and spread of 1.508 from the example above it.

**Why we normalize at all**, as a second table of raw versus rescaled ranges. Train counts reach 94 while cancellation rates never pass 0.44, so without rescaling the model would weigh the biggest numbers as the most important. It also notes that the delay spike survives at 6.18, rather than being flattened.

**How numbers become tokens**, as a five-step chain: 168 points, cut into 42 four-hour patches, encoded to 128 dimensions each, projected up to the 896 the base model uses, ending as 126 vectors sitting between the words of the question. I verified each of those numbers against the installed code and the model config rather than quoting the paper.

It closes on the thing worth understanding: only the encoder and projector are learned from scratch, 11 million parameters, and the language model is barely touched. Teaching a small translator to speak a frozen model's language is the whole idea behind a time-series language model.

ChannelWhat it measuresWhy it earns a slotComputed as
Mean delayAverage lateness of every train touching the station that hour, in minutes.The thing we predict, and the thing a passenger actually feels.avg(delay_in_min)
Cancellation rateShare of that hour's stops that were cancelled.A cancelled train leaves the delay average, so delay alone flatters an hour where the line collapsed. This is the correction.avg(is_canceled)

input.content:
error404.ai / Temporal AI Challenge / two minutes

Give a language model a sense of when the trains run late

Speaking spine for the jury pitch. Six beats, two minutes, one graphic each. Every number on this page comes from a run that already happened.

0:00Hook

226,000,000

stop records · free · CC BY 4.0

Every stop of every German train since July 2024 is public. Nobody else here is touching it. The organizers' own dataset list has wearables, hearts, sleep, machines and ships. No rail.

If asked why rail: it is the one temporal domain in the room that every single person in the audience has personally waited on.

0:20The move

A single train visits twenty stops. That is too short to model. So we flip it: a station has a pulse, one week of it, sampled every hour.

Three channels, not one. Delay is what people feel. Cancellations correct it, because a cancelled train quietly leaves the average. Train count is the confidence, since twenty minutes over two night trains is not twenty minutes over eighty at rush hour.

0:40The task

Then we ask about hours it has never seen. Nothing here was labelled by hand or by another model — the answer and the reasoning are both computed.

In · one week, three channels

Mean delay2.01 min avg

Cancellation rate6.7%

Trains per hour64.6

Mean delay over the next six hours?

Out · reasoning, then answer

The past week averaged 2.0 minutes. At the same hours of day it averaged 1.8. The six hours that follow come in below that seasonal level. Answer: 1.17

1:05The signal

Is there anything to learn? The network resets every dawn. Delay builds all day, peaks after midnight as long-distance trains finally arrive, then falls to under two minutes at six.

840
0002 06 12 1823

Mean delay in minutes by hour of day, over 1,500 training windows. Peak 11.4 at 02:00, low 1.9 at 06:00.

1:25The honesty

We split on two axes so we cannot fool ourselves. Eight of forty stations never appear in training, and the test period starts a full week after training ends. We report all four cells, not the flattering one.

Trained era
Later era
Seen
stations
Ceilingknows place and era
New weeksknown place
Held-out
stations
New placesknown era
The real numberneither ever seen

1:45The close

The piece that was missing

OpenTSLM and TimeNet come from the same lab and do not talk to each other. Nothing carried a standardised dataset into training. We wrote that connector, and it knows nothing about trains, so it works for anyone's data.

674 sfull training run
7,338tasks generated
levelforecast vs baseline
not yetbeating it

Close on the honest line: the pipeline is finished and measured, the model is eleven minutes old and matches its baseline rather than beating it. Next run starts from a pretrained encoder instead of random weights.

Detail, methodology and the full four-cell results live in the companion brief. Data: the public Deutsche Bahn scrape, CC BY 4.0.

Six beats with a timecode on each, styled as a departure board. Hook on 226 million public stop records that nobody else here is using. The station pulse with the week chart. Each beat carries one line to say and a small note for the questions that will follow.

- **Mean delay** is what a passenger feels, and the thing we predict.
- **Cancellation rate** is the correction, because a cancelled train silently leaves the delay average and makes a collapsed line look fine.
- **Trains per hour** is the confidence, since twenty minutes across two night trains is not twenty minutes across eighty at rush hour.

Plus why three and not more: each one changes how you read the other two, and all three fall out of columns already on every row. Weather and delay propagation between stations were considered and cut.

I left the brief long on purpose since you said to keep it. It is the reference document behind the pitch, and the pitch page points at it.

You are right, and the reason it reads as nothing is that there is no idea in it yet. I built a mechanism and then dressed it up. Here are the three answers plainly.

## What exists right now

Four scripts that chain together, plus one trained model.

1. Download German train punctuality data. Public and free, 226 million stop records.
2. Reshape it into one week of hourly numbers per station: how late trains were, how many were cancelled, how many ran.
3. For each week, automatically write a question and its correct answer, plus the reasoning that leads to it. No human labelling.
4. Feed that to a small language model, train it, and measure it against a dumb baseline.

It runs end to end. The model writes a sentence of reasoning and ends with a number. That number is currently about as good as guessing the recent average. So: the plumbing is finished and measured, and there is no result worth showing.

## The idea, which was missing

The three questions I picked were arbitrary. I chose them because their answers were computable, not because anyone wants them answered. That is the hole you are feeling.

Here is the idea I would commit to: **a buffer advisor.** You say "I change trains at Köln at 18:40 on Thursday" and it answers in words. Something like: this station runs about five minutes late at that hour, which is worse than its own weekly average, so leave fifteen minutes rather than eight.

Why that one. Every judge in the room has missed a connection, so it needs no explaining. It is answerable from exactly the data we already model. And it justifies using a language model at all, because the output is advice with a reason and a caveat, not a single number a regression could produce.

That reframes our three questions into parts of one answer: what delay to expect, whether it is unusual, and which hours to avoid.

Seventeen hours to the submit target, two of which are buffer.

error404.ai · Temporal AI Challenge · status and plan

Where we are, and the fifteen hours left

The pipeline is finished and measured. The product idea is not settled, and that is the decision blocking everything else.

Part one

What exists right now

Four scripts that chain together, and one trained model. In plain terms:

  1. Download German train punctuality data. Public and free. 226 million stop records since July 2024.

  2. Reshape it into one week of hourly numbers per station. Three numbers each hour: how late trains ran, how many were cancelled, how many passed through.

  3. Automatically write a question, its correct answer, and the reasoning that leads there. Nothing is labelled by a human or by another model. The answers are arithmetic on hours the model is not shown.

  4. Train a small language model on that, and score it against a dumb baseline. Eleven minutes on one GPU produces 7,338 training examples worth of learning.

runsend to end
674 sfull training
levelvs baseline
noproduct idea yet

Honest status: the model writes a sentence of reasoning and ends with a number. That number is currently about as good as guessing the recent average. The plumbing is done. There is no result worth showing.

Part two · for the team to decide

The idea, which was missing

The three questions in the pipeline were picked because their answers were computable, not because anyone wants them answered. That is the hole. Here is the idea worth committing to.

A buffer advisor

You name a station and a time. It tells you, in words, how much slack to leave.

A person asks

“I change trains at Köln Hbf at 18:40 on Thursday. How much buffer do I need?”

The model answers

Köln runs about 7.9 minutes late on average, and the early evening is one of its worse stretches rather than one of its better ones. Delay there is still climbing at that hour and does not ease until after midnight. Leave fifteen minutes, not eight.

Illustration of the output we are building toward, using real measured figures. The model does not produce this yet.

Why this one. Every judge in the room has missed a connection, so it needs no explaining. It is answerable from exactly the data we already model. And it justifies using a language model at all, because the output is advice with a reason and a caveat, not a single number a plain forecaster could produce.

It also rescues the three questions. They stop being arbitrary and become the parts of one answer: what delay to expect, whether that is unusual for this place, and which hours to avoid.

Part three

Why the advice is possible at all

Because delay is not random. It follows the same shape every day, and that shape is what the model has to learn.

840
0002 06 12 1823

Average delay in minutes by hour of day, measured across 1,500 weeks of station history. Lowest at 06:00 with 1.9 minutes, when the timetable starts clean. Climbs all day, and peaks at 11.4 after midnight as long-distance trains finally arrive. The green bar is 18:00, the hour in the question above.

Part four

The next fifteen hours

Seventeen hours to the submit target, of which two are buffer.

WhenWhatWho
now → +2h Lock the user and the one demo sentence Rewrite the three questions to serve it, regenerate the data. Herit, Jonas
+2 → +5h Train from a pretrained checkpoint Instead of random weights. Needs one licence click. Add the text-only baseline, which is the comparison judges will ask for. Jonas
+5 → +8h Build the demo Pick a station and an hour, see the week, get the advice, with the baseline beside it. Akshat
+8 → +11h Final evaluation and a second run Score across the four leakage splits, fix the two weak questions. Gaurav, Yash
+11 → +13h Deck and dry runProtect this time. Herit
+13 → +15h BufferDo not spend it early. —

The one decision blocking the rest. Agree the buffer advisor, or name a different user. Everything in the table after the first row assumes an answer.

One thing worth keeping in the pitch either way: OpenTSLM and TimeNet come from the same lab and do not connect to each other. We wrote the 128 lines that join them, and they know nothing about trains, so any dataset can use them. Full methodology and the four-cell results are in the companion brief.

## Existing Applications and Tools

Bahnvorhersage is a free tool designed to mirror the interface of the DB Navigator and help users identify the most reliable train connections. Developed by two students from Tübingen, this innovative project utilises an AI model trained on approximately 700 GB of railway connection data and predicts the likelihood of passengers making one or more connections.

Additionally, DB Delay Predictor analyzes past Deutsche Bahn journeys to show how likely your train is to run late.

## Deutsche Bahn's Official Machine Learning Approach

Historical data is fed into machine-learning algorithms to "train" forecasting models that identify delay patterns, and the models are then combined with real-time data to predict current train movements. A machine learning algorithm calculates expected arrival and departure times for long-distance and local trains from mass data (Big Data), and the times are communicated to all customer channels.

Influencing variables—so-called features—are calculated which are expected to explain the delay as well as possible, such as the current delay at the time the forecast is generated or the travel times planned in the timetable.

Based on my search results, here's what the benchmarking research shows about whether LLMs beat classical forecasters like gradient boosting:

## Key Findings

**The evidence is mixed and contested:**

### LLM-Based Claims
Some research shows that Time-LLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art forecasting methods by large margins across multiple benchmarks and settings, especially in few-shot and zero-shot scenarios. Additionally, LLMTime achieved higher likelihoods and CRPS values in zero-shot evaluation than dedicated time series models like ARIMA, TCNs, and N-HiTS.

Other research demonstrated that LLM-based frameworks significantly reduce mean absolute error and root mean square error compared with ARIMA, Prophet, and Temporal Fusion Transformer benchmarks.

### Critical Counterargument
However, a more recent critical analysis challenges these claims. One study found that popular LLM-based time series forecasters perform the same or worse than basic LLM-free ablations, yet require orders of magnitude more compute. Notably, when researchers shuffled input time series, there was no appreciable change in performance, and LLMs did not help forecasting in few-shot settings with 10% of the training data.

## Gradient Boosting's Track Record
Separately, in the M5 competition (2020), on 42,840 related retail series with prices, promotions and calendar effects, gradient boosting dominated the leaderboard. Additionally, gradient boosting has shown excellent performance in forecasting challenges.

The comparison between LLMs and gradient boosting specifically remains an active area of research with competing claims about relative effectiveness.

Part four

Are we adding anything?

Two questions a judge will ask, answered honestly, because being caught out on either would cost more than admitting them.

Does this already exist? Yes.

  • BahnvorhersageTwo students in Tübingen. Trained on roughly 700 GB of connection data, mirrors the DB Navigator interface, and tells you how likely you are to make your connection. This is our buffer advisor, already built and free.
  • DB Delay PredictorReads past journeys and shows how likely your specific train is to run late.
  • Deutsche Bahn themselvesRun machine-learned delay forecasting in production, combining historical patterns with live positions, feeding every customer channel.

So we are not first and must not claim to be. What none of them do is explain. They return a number or a probability. Ours returns the reasoning that produced it, and one model answers several different question shapes rather than one.

Is a language model even the right tool? Probably not, for the number.

A gradient-boosted tree on hand-built features would very likely beat us on accuracy at a fraction of the compute. That family won the M5 forecasting competition outright. A 2024 paper went further and found popular language-model forecasters matching or losing to language-model-free versions while costing orders of magnitude more, and that shuffling the input series barely changed their results.

Our own numbers currently side with the sceptics. We match a trivial baseline, we do not beat it. Saying that first is stronger than being asked.

The argument that survives is not accuracy. It is that one model takes several different questions in plain language, returns an answer with a rationale a person can check, and can absorb written context that a tree has no way to read. Whether that is worth the compute is exactly the open question this challenge is about.

What we should do about it: add a gradient-boosted baseline to our own results table. It is an hour of work and it is the comparison anyone who knows the field will ask for. If it beats us, we show that too.

# Deutsche Bahn Train Data

This dataset contains public historical data from Deutsche Bahn, the largest German train company. It includes train schedules, delays, and cancellations from stations across Germany.

For more info visit the project page at GitHub: https://github.com/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data

## Dataset Structure

### Monthly Processed Data

The monthly processed data is located in `monthly_processed_data/` and contains files named `data-YYYY-MM.parquet`.

**Schema:**

| Column | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `station_name` | string | Name of the station |
| `xml_station_name` | string | Station name from the XML response |
| `eva` | string | EVA station number (unique identifier) |
| `train_number` | string | Train number / Zugnummer, the raw `tl.n` value identifying a specific train run (e.g., "123", "12603"). Combine with `train_type` for a label like "ICE 123" |
| `line_number` | string | Line number / Liniennummer, the raw `ar.l`/`dp.l` value identifying the route, non-unique (e.g., "RB23", "14"); null for long-distance trains (ICE/IC/EC) where the API provides no line |

| `delay_in_min` | integer | Delay in minutes |
| `time` | timestamp | Actual arrival or departure time |
| `arrival_is_canceled` | boolean | Whether the arrival at the train stop was canceled |
| `departure_is_canceled` | boolean | Whether the departure from the train stop was canceled |
| `train_type` | string | Type of train (e.g., "ICE", "IC", "RE") |
| `train_line_ride_id` | string | Unique identifier for the train ride |
| `train_line_station_num` | integer | Station number in the train's route |
| `arrival_planned_time` | timestamp | Planned arrival time |

import duckdb, re, collections
URL=("https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/"
     "raw_data/year=2026/month=8/day=15/date_2026-08-15_hour_14_15_16_17_18_19.parquet")
con=duckdb.connect(); con.execute("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
print(con.execute(f"SELECT api_name, count(*) n FROM read_parquet('{URL}') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC").df().to_string(index=False))
rows=con.execute(f"SELECT response_data FROM read_parquet('{URL}') WHERE api_name LIKE '%fchg%' AND length(response_data)>2000 LIMIT 40").fetchall()
print("\nsampled", len(rows), "fchg responses")
codes=collections.Counter(); has_msg=0
for (xml,) in rows:
    ms=re.findall(r'<m [^>]*>', xml or "")
    if ms: has_msg+=1
    for m in ms:
        c=re.search(r'\bc="(\d+)"', m)
        t=re.search(r'\bt="(\w+)"', m)
        if c: codes[(t.group(1) if t else "?", c.group(1))]+=1
print("responses containing <m> messages:", has_msg)
print("top (type, code) pairs:", codes.most_common(12))
for (xml,) in rows:
    m=re.search(r'<m [^>]*t="[hq]"[^>]*>', xml or "")
    if m: print("\nexample message element:\n ", m.group(0)[:300]); break
EOF

import duckdb, re, collections
URL=("https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/"
     "raw_data/year=2026/month=8/day=15/date_2026-08-15_hour_14_15_16_17_18_19.parquet")
con=duckdb.connect(); con.execute("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
rows=con.execute(f"SELECT response_data FROM read_parquet('{URL}') WHERE api_name LIKE '%fchg%' LIMIT 900").fetchall()
cats=collections.Counter(); texts=collections.Counter(); dcodes=collections.Counter()
for (xml,) in rows:
    if not xml: continue
    for c in re.findall(r'\bcat="([^"]{1,60})"', xml): cats[c]+=1
    for t in re.findall(r'\bint="([^"]{1,90})"', xml): texts[t]+=1
    for m in re.findall(r'<m [^>]*t="d"[^>]*>', xml):
        c=re.search(r'\bc="(\d+)"', m)
        if c: dcodes[c.group(1)]+=1
print("scanned", len(rows), "responses")
print("\nfree-text categories (cat=):")
for k,v in cats.most_common(12): print(f"  {v:6}  {k}")
print("\nfree-text internal messages (int=):")
for k,v in texts.most_common(8): print(f"  {v:6}  {k[:80]}")
print("\ndelay cause codes (t=d):", dcodes.most_common(14))
EOF
uv run --quiet --with duckdb --with pandas python raw_cats.py 2>&1 | tail -32

Here's what I can tell you from the search results:

"Verspätung eines vorausfahrenden Zuges" (delay of a preceding train) causes wait times and occurs on certain routes, where the train must reduce its speed due to another train ahead.

Regarding the API itself, the Deutsche Bahn Timetables API is available through the official Deutsche Bahn developer portal at developers.deutschebahn.com. However, the specific numeric codes for the "c=" parameter and their complete mapping to delay cause descriptions don't appear to be publicly documented in the search results.

The closest reference I found was a technical document from the German railway authority (Bundesnetzagentur) that mentions delay cause codes (Kodierungen) are assigned numbers ranging from 10 to 95, but it doesn't provide the complete mapping list or confirm that code 43 specifically represents "Verspätung eines vorausfahrenden Zuges."

To access the complete and authoritative mapping of these delay cause codes, you would likely need to:
1. Register for the Deutsche Bahn developer API at developers.deutschebahn.com
2. Consult the official API documentation
3. Check community projects on GitHub that have reverse-engineered this mapping

content.text:
Yes, but not in the table we are using. This is the most useful thing I have found today.

**The processed data has no cause.** All 18 columns are timing, identity and cancellation flags. Nothing about why.

**The raw partition has it.** That directory stores the untouched XML from the DB changes endpoint, and those responses carry message elements with delay causes. Scanning 900 responses from six hours of 15 August:

| Signal | What I found |
|---|---|
| Delay cause codes | 43 dominates at 7,024, then 48, 31, 45, 36, 38, 42, 8, 34, 5 |
| Free-text category | Information 17,022, Störung 11,999, Bauarbeiten 5,816 |

The numeric codes need a lookup to become words. Deutsche Bahn does not publish that table anywhere easy to find, but community projects carry the German strings, and they are exactly what you would want: delay of a preceding train, signal fault, points fault, person on the track, construction work, short-notice staff shortage, weather disruption.

**Why this matters more than it sounds.** The challenge's own ideal data profile asks for a dataset with time series and text reasoning over it, and suggests generating the text with a language model if you lack it. That is precisely what we are doing now, and it is our weakest point. With causes, the text is real and written by the operator. That turns "we manufactured annotations" into "we paired a real signal with real operational text", which is a different class of dataset.

**Three honest caveats.** The messages attach to individual train runs, not to our station-hour aggregate, so joining them takes care. Code 43 is by far the most common and means a preceding train was late, which is a knock-on effect rather than a root cause, so the causes are partly circular for prediction. And the free-text category has only three values, so the richness lives in the codes, not the words.

**Cost.** You do not need the whole raw partition. Counting causes per station and hour is a small aggregate on top of the same remote query pattern we already use. I would put it at about an hour, and it is the highest-value hour available right now, ahead of anything on the current plan except naming the user.

Want me to extract it and add a fourth channel plus the cause text, and put this on the page?

Sources:
- [piebro/deutsche-bahn-data](https://github.com/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data) and its [dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/blob/main/README.md)
- [deutsche-bahn-delay-reasons](https://github.com/barafael/deutsche-bahn-delay-reasons), which carries the German cause strings
- [Ril 420.9001, the official coding of additional delays](https://www.bundesnetzagentur.de/DE/Beschlusskammern/1_GZ/BK10-GZ/2018/2018_0200bis0299/BK10-18-0202/Anlagen/SNB_2020_IIIIIIII_Anlage%206.5.1%20Ril%20420.9001%2015.12.2019%20clean.pdf?__blob=publicationFile&v=1)

content.text: Good challenge, and it is testable rather than arguable. Let me measure whether a station-hour mean is one thing or a blend of unlike regimes.

input.command:
cd /Users/jonasstenglein/.claude/jobs/51710a92/tmp/db && cat > pooling.py <<'EOF'
import duckdb
U=("https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/"
   "monthly_processed_data/data-2026-08.parquet")
c=duckdb.connect(); c.execute("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
c.execute(f"""CREATE TABLE s AS
SELECT station_name, train_type, line_number, delay_in_min AS d,
       date_trunc('hour', time) AS h, extract('hour' FROM time) AS hod
FROM read_parquet('{U}')
WHERE station_name IN ('Köln Hbf','Hamburg Hbf','München Hbf','Berlin Hbf','Frankfurt(Main)Hbf')
  AND delay_in_min IS NOT NULL""")
print("rows:", c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM s").fetchone()[0])

print("\n=== how heterogeneous is a station? distinct lines and types ===")
print(c.execute("""SELECT station_name, count(DISTINCT train_type) AS types,
 count(DISTINCT line_number) AS lines, count(*) AS stops FROM s GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY stops DESC""").df().to_string(index=False))

print("\n=== mean delay by train type, Köln Hbf ===")
print(c.execute("""SELECT train_type, count(*) AS n, round(avg(d),2) AS mean_delay,
 round(stddev(d),2) AS sd FROM s WHERE station_name='Köln Hbf'
 GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*)>500 ORDER BY mean_delay DESC""").df().to_string(index=False))

print("\n=== variance decomposition (all 5 stations) ===")
print(c.execute("""
WITH tot AS (SELECT var_pop(d) v FROM s),
 sh AS (SELECT station_name, h, avg(d) m, count(*) n FROM s GROUP BY 1,2),
 betw AS (SELECT var_pop(m) v FROM sh),
 sht AS (SELECT station_name, h, train_type, avg(d) m FROM s GROUP BY 1,2,3),
 betw2 AS (SELECT var_pop(m) v FROM sht)
SELECT round((SELECT v FROM tot),1) AS total_var,
       round((SELECT v FROM betw),1) AS var_of_station_hour_means,
       round((SELECT v FROM betw2),1) AS var_of_station_hour_type_means,
       round(100.0*(SELECT v FROM betw)/(SELECT v FROM tot),1) AS pct_kept_pooling_station,
       round(100.0*(SELECT v FROM betw2)/(SELECT v FROM tot),1) AS pct_kept_splitting_by_type
""").df().to_string(index=False))
EOF
uv run --quiet --with duckdb --with pandas python pooling.py 2>&1 | tail -32

FROM read_parquet('{U}')

print("=== correct variance decomposition (share of delay variance explained) ===")
for name, cols in [("station + hour", "station_name, hod"),
                   ("station + hour + train type", "station_name, hod, train_type")]:
    r=c.execute(f"""
    WITH g AS (SELECT {cols}, avg(d) m, count(*) n FROM s GROUP BY ALL),
         j AS (SELECT s.d, g.m FROM s JOIN g USING ({cols}))

print("\n=== is the 02:00 peak real, or just which trains run then? (Köln Hbf) ===")
print(c.execute("""
SELECT hod,
  round(avg(d),2) AS pooled_mean,
  round(100.0*sum(CASE WHEN train_type IN ('ICE','IC','EC') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/count(*),1) AS pct_longdistance,
  round(avg(CASE WHEN train_type IN ('ICE','IC','EC') THEN d END),2) AS longdist_mean,
  round(avg(CASE WHEN train_type IN ('S','RB','RE') THEN d END),2) AS regional_mean,
  count(*) AS stops
FROM s WHERE station_name='Köln Hbf' AND hod IN (2,6,12,18,22) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""").df().to_string(index=False))
EOF

content.text:
You are right, and it is worse than a nuance. Two measurements settle it.

**Pooling by station throws away most of the structure.**

| Grouping | Share of delay variance explained |
|---|---|
| Station and hour | 3.3% |
| Station, hour and train type | 23.6% |

Adding train type multiplies the explanatory power sevenfold. At Köln in August, an ICE averaged 16.4 minutes late and an RB 4.2 at the same station. Our single hourly number is a blend of those.

**And it distorts the headline claim I put on both pages.** I checked whether the 02:00 peak was just a change in which trains run at night. It is not, but the real mechanism is narrower than I said:

| Hour at Köln | Pooled | Long distance | Regional |
|---|---|---|---|
| 02:00 | 8.6 | 33.5 | 4.9 |
| 06:00 | 5.0 | 5.9 | 4.1 |
| 12:00 | 6.0 | 9.7 | 3.9 |
| 18:00 | 9.4 | 17.0 | 6.8 |
| 22:00 | 10.8 | 29.6 | 5.2 |

The long-distance share of traffic is essentially identical at 02:00 and 06:00, so this is not a mix effect. But the daily cycle is almost entirely a long-distance phenomenon. Those trains swing from 5.9 to 33.5 minutes across the day. Regional trains barely move, from 3.9 to 6.8. Pooling compresses a sixfold swing into a twofold one and implies the whole network behaves the same way. It does not.

**What I would change.** Make the unit of analysis station and train category, rather than station alone. Three categories, long distance, regional and S-Bahn, gives about 120 series instead of 40, which is still small. Not line number: Köln has 21 lines and München 41, too sparse, and it is null for long-distance trains anyway.

content.text:
Measured properly, your intuition is right but it lands on a different column than you would expect. Here is the honest test: fit group averages on the first half of August, score them on the second half.

| Grouping | In sample | Out of sample | Groups |
|---|---|---|---|
| Station and hour | 3.3% | 3.1% | 72 |
| Station, hour, train type | 23.6% | 17.9% | 638 |
| Station, hour, line number | 64.9% | 4.2% | 1,458 |
| Station, hour, train number | 77.5% | 28.3% | 8,418 |

**Line number was a mirage.** It looked like the dominant factor at 64.9% and collapses to 4.2% when validated. That was my metric fitting noise, the third time today I have had to correct that same mistake. Knowing it is RE9 rather than RB27 tells you almost nothing you did not already know from the station and the hour.

**Why it fails.** A line label averages over every service on that route all day, in both directions. RE9 at 07:00 outbound and RE9 at 23:00 inbound are different animals wearing the same badge. There is also a contaminant: the line column is empty for all long-distance trains, which is exactly where the big delays are, so the test is kinder to regional lines than it looks.

**What does survive is the individual scheduled train.** Train number holds 28.3% out of sample, the best of any grouping. A specific service has a persistent signature, because it always runs the same route at the same time and inherits the same upstream problems. That is also why the analysis platforms you are thinking of are built per train, not per line. Zugfinder gives you a page for ICE 43 specifically.

**So the recommendation changes, but not to lines.** Split the series by train category. It is the robust choice at 17.9% and it needs only three groups. Do not split by line.

Train number is too thin for its own series, at eight observations per group in half a month. The right use is as context the model reads rather than a series it gets: tell it the service identity and its historical signature in the prompt. That is something a language model can use and a tree cannot, which is a rare point in our favour on the earlier question of whether the language model earns its place.

Do you want me to make the category split now, or keep pulling on the per-train angle first?

content.text:
Both go in, and the series part is already embeddings. That is worth unpacking because the answer is "that is exactly how it works", with one real gap.

**At prediction time the prompt is a single sequence of vectors.** Some come from words, some from numbers.

The words go through the model's normal vocabulary lookup. The 168 hourly numbers per channel go through our encoder and projector, which turn them into 896-dimensional vectors in the same space the word embeddings live in. By the time the language model sees the prompt, it cannot tell which vectors came from text and which came from the signal. They are interleaved: some words, then 42 vectors for delay, then more words, then 42 for cancellations, and so on.

**Nothing is precomputed or stored.** There is no vector database and no embedding cache. You hand it a window of numbers, and the encoder embeds them in that instant. So feeding up-to-date data is automatic. Pull the last 168 hours from the live feed, pass them in, and you get an answer grounded in this morning rather than in August. No retraining, no re-indexing.

| Fixed after training | Chosen per request |
|---|---|
| Encoder and projector weights | The window of numbers |
| The LoRA adaptation | The question text |
| The base language model | Any context text you add |

**What is genuinely missing, and is your opening.** Only numbers and our own question text go in today. Two things could join them, and both are text the model would read directly.

The first is the delay causes I found in the raw data yesterday. Signal fault, construction work, person on the track. That is real operational text describing the same hours as the signal, and it is the pairing the challenge brief actually asks for.

The second is retrieval. Look up the three most similar past weeks for that station and put their outcomes in the prompt. That is not done and would be a genuine addition rather than a tweak.

**One practical catch for the demo.** Our downloaded data stops on 31 August. Truly live input needs the DB timetable API, which needs a developer key and a registration wait. For the pitch I would run against a fixed recent date and say plainly that the live feed is a key away, rather than burn hours on registration.

`TSLM` is also redundant here, since the whole repo is the time-series language model challenge. Amending to something plainer.
